text:
I keep three occurrences distinct: **A** is the P7 excerpt on criticism targets; **B** is the P9 excerpt on local alternatives, global availability, and the conditional compatibility objection; **J** is the construct occurrence supplied above. The following is a proposed successor **J′**, not a replacement of the historical J, not an amendment to A or B, and not an installed language extension. No claim of executed repair or creativity is made here.

## Decision on the criticism

The criticism is partly successful, but it does not establish that J’s substantive answer fails. It establishes a defect in J’s framing.

J says that P7’s list lacks a slot for “criticizing a commitment the snapshot does not carry.” That is too broad. P7 already names “the assumption that logical time is meaningful.” That is an assumption the description relies on and is not a record the snapshot carries. So P7’s list already contains an assumption-target, at least by example. J’s announced novelty cannot be the carried/not-carried split as such.

What J actually needs is narrower: the difference between criticizing an assumption the description *makes* and criticizing a relation the description’s vocabulary *cannot draw*. The compatibility objection in B has both aspects. B’s conditional warehouse claim — “booking A’s high alternative might be incompatible with booking B’s high alternative if they share a physical resource not named in the snapshot” — is an assertable claim. If the shared resource and the incompatible assignment are observed, that claim becomes a criticism of a presupposition: that cross-booking alternatives are jointly unconstrained beyond capacity. That is locatable in P7’s assumption target. B’s further gloss — “The snapshot does not name physical resources, so this incompatibility is invisible” — is a different speech act. It criticizes expressive scope, not a false record or rule.

So the criticism correctly separates B’s conditional factual claim from B’s meta-observation about invisibility. It also correctly weakens J’s claim that P7 has no slot for B’s objection. In the factual reading, B’s objection can be an assumption-target criticism once its condition is met. In the expressive-limit reading, P7’s list may indeed need a further target, but J has not shown that P7’s “snapshot as a whole” cannot be stretched to cover it, nor has J cleanly distinguished that target from the fifth item.

The secondary criticism is also partly sound. B does mark interval construction and correlation loss with “but intervals lose correlations.” J’s stronger claim that B “runs together” local and joint loss overstates the textual situation. The genuine addition is repair asymmetry: keeping per-booking alternatives addresses the local loss but does not address the joint loss. That addition survives, but it should not be stated as if B failed to name the distinction at all.

A successor is therefore warranted, but only as a correction of J’s announced framing and of the secondary overstatement. J’s core claims remain: that the compatibility objection can survive full acceptance of rules and records; that its cost depends on whether “global availability” is a marginal summary or a joint feasibility claim; that local alternatives, aggregation, bounds, and cross-booking correlation have different roles; and that further observation or interpretation is needed before the objection has a determinate target.

## Proposed successor J′

**A’s taxonomy already includes assumptions.** P7 lists a reconstruction rule, a particular record, a booking’s history, the snapshot as a whole, and the assumption that logical time is meaningful. The list should be read as having at least three families:

1. **Carried claims**: a rule, a record, a booking history, a snapshot-wide consistency or aggregation claim.
2. **Presuppositions**: assumptions the description relies on, such as the meaningfulness of logical time, and — if assumed — the joint independence of bookings except through capacity.
3. **Expressive limits**: relations the snapshot vocabulary cannot state, such as unnamed physical-resource sharing.

The compatibility objection in B is not one thing. It has a conditional factual aspect and an expressive-limit aspect.

As a **conditional factual claim**, it says: if bookings A and B share a physical resource not named in the snapshot, and if an assignment shows that A’s high alternative and B’s high alternative cannot both hold, then the cross-booking independence presupposition is false. This is a criticism of an assumption the description relies on. It is not a criticism of a rule as such, nor of a particular record, nor of the data as corrupt or late. It can be raised while accepting every rule and every delivered record. When its condition is met, it is locatable under P7’s assumption target.

As an **expressive-limit claim**, it says: the snapshot does not name physical resources, so this constraint is invisible. This is not the same as saying the snapshot is inconsistent or that a rule is wrong. It says that the vocabulary cannot record the relation that would make the joint combination permissible or impermissible. If “global availability” is only a marginal summary — capacity minus per-booking reservations, with bounds — this expressive limit does not change the arithmetic endpoints. If “global availability” is offered as a statement of what can be jointly realized, then the expressive limit matters, and no refinement within the per-booking representation repairs it. The same objection is therefore free or costly depending on what the account claims to answer.

**Local loss and joint loss must be separated by role.** The local loss is that tied greatest-revision alternatives for one booking collapse to min and max, so the interval omits per-booking structure. Keeping the alternatives addresses that loss. The joint loss is that even a full product of per-booking possibilities can include a combination — high-A with high-B — that an unnamed shared resource would exclude. Keeping per-booking alternatives does not address the joint loss. B names both an interval construction and a loss of correlations, but it does not state this repair asymmetry. That asymmetry is the addition.

**The protected uses remain distinguishable.** Questioning a rule differs from questioning a record. Accepting or rejecting rules and data in different combinations remains possible. B’s cross-booking incompatibility remains a conditional possibility, not an observation, until a resource-sharing relation and an incompatible assignment are supplied. Local alternatives, aggregation, bounds, and correlation objections keep different roles: alternatives represent per-booking unresolved possibilities; aggregation produces a summary; bounds give marginal endpoints; correlation objections concern joint realizability. Exposing alternatives and objecting to downstream resolution remain disputed positions. J′ does not resolve that dispute. It says only that exposing per-booking alternatives addresses the local loss and does not by itself answer the joint loss; a downstream policy might handle correlation, but that remains a contested division of labor.

**What would matter further.** Two observations, or a decision in place of the second, would change the situation. One is about the warehouse: a resource-sharing relation plus an assignment showing that certain high alternatives cannot co-occur. The other is about use: whether the consumer of availability is asking for a marginal summary or a joint feasibility test. Neither is contained in A, B, or the snapshot. Without the first, the incompatibility remains a possibility the snapshot cannot rule in or out. Without the second, it is not determinate whether the account was overclaiming.

## What the criticized distinction changes in the organization

The criticized distinction forces J′ to replace J’s broad “carried vs not-carried” novelty with a narrower one: **presupposition the description makes** vs **expressive limit the description cannot draw**. It also forces the compatibility objection to be split into a conditional factual version, which lands under P7’s assumption target when its condition is met, and an expressive-limit version, which is a different target and may or may not be covered by “the snapshot as a whole.” Finally, it weakens the local/joint claim from “B runs them together” to “B names both but does not articulate the repair asymmetry.”

The protected source meanings remain: rule criticism is not record criticism; different combinations of accepting and rejecting rules and records remain possible; B’s incompatibility is conditional, not observed; local alternatives, aggregation, bounds, and correlation objections have different roles; and the dispute over exposing alternatives versus objecting to downstream resolution is not settled by J′.

Any language extension — for example a resource relation, a possible-worlds set, or a separate target vocabulary for expressive limits — is a separate proposed object. It is not installed here and should not be treated as part of the frozen carrier. J remains a distinct historical occurrence; A and B remain distinct source occurrences; J′ is only a proposed successor in prose, offered for the current route to carry.
